title: The strategy behind those Black Friday deals
description:
We get the inside scoop in how a Black Friday discount deal comes together.

A MARTÍNEZ, HOST: If you are shopping today for Black Friday discounts, Planet Money's Kenny Malone wants you to know about the backstory for big deals.KENNY MALONE, BYLINE: If you walk into a Target today, you will likely see a display of 50%-off games, including "Sell Me A Sasquatch," a purple-colored game secretly about economics that we have been making as a reporting project. And this Black Friday placement and sale has been in the works for almost a year.MARTIN MARECHAL: We probably pitched it earlier this year - like, January or February.MALONE: Martin Marechal is a VP with the company Exploding Kittens, which publishes our game. And his pitch to the big-box retailer was - Exploding Kittens makes games for different age groups that would look good together and will all start from the same price point.MARECHAL: They like to have a story. Sometimes price is the story, especially for Black Friday.MALONE: The story is all the same price?MARECHAL: It's game under 20, you know?MALONE: Used to be 20, now isn't. That's the story. Yeah.DAISY RITZ: Yeah, yeah, yeah.MALONE: Yeah.RITZ: Yeah.MALONE: That last voice there is Exploding Kittens' VP of brand, Daisy Ritz. And yeah. They have agreed to sell our game for half price. But the calculation is that this Black Friday sale gets our game out there, 'cause games are one of these products that grow exponentially from network effects.RITZ: So there is this webbing effect that can happen with a great game where it starts to spread. We just need to ignite that to start spreading.MALONE: But not all product categories may have the same goals on Black Friday.DINESH GAURI: Now, for products like television or...MALONE: Blenders? Let's talk about blenders in there.GAURI: Yeah. So I think...MALONE: Dinesh Gauri is a marketing professor at the University of Buffalo - has studied retail discounting. And he says maybe a manufacturer's trying to get rid of old models of a product, or maybe they're trying to build brand loyalty. Or maybe, Gauri says, selling us the physical product is just opening a door. Like, think about smart TVs. Those companies can make money off of us even after we buy the TV by collecting and monetizing our data.GAURI: So then TV becomes a medium by which - like, they can basically advertise through there.MALONE: There's a secondary business model here that could make up for the fact that they sold the TV at a discount.GAURI: Yes. There is.MALONE: Companies will often have minimum advertised price policies for retailers. And to do these Black Friday sales, they may carve out little exceptions that say, for one week only, we're cool selling our game for, you know, ten bucks instead of 20. Although, says Martin Marechal from Exploding Kittens, sometimes store-to-store price matching can mess things up.MARECHAL: Yeah. I mean, it's every sales guy's nightmare.MALONE: These days, Target and Walmart and Amazon have systems to immediately match competitor prices. And even if our sale on "Sell Me A Sasquatch" is supposed to expire after a week, Marechal says it doesn't mean the price-matching standoff always unwinds perfectly.MARECHAL: Just have to - after the deals are done, the systems still look at each other and get stuck. So sometimes you get the price stuck for longer than you want.MALONE: Oh, no.MARECHAL: And - yeah.MALONE: Don't say that. No.MARECHAL: Yeah. So it's very tricky.MALONE: Like it or not, every Black Friday discount strategy comes with its own risks and rewards.Kenny Malone, NPR News.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)MARTÍNEZ: Find the whole series on designing and manufacturing a party game based on Nobel Prize-winning economics in the Planet Money podcast feed.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC) Copyright © 2026 NPR.
